## Sharing your environment

This is the payoff for everything in [uv: projects](0530-virtual-environments-python-uv-projects.qmd).

Your collaborator clones your repository.
They get `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`, `.python-version`,
and your code,
but no `.venv/`.
They run one command:

```bash
uv sync
```

```out
Using CPython 3.14.3
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Resolved 6 packages in 21ms
Installed 5 packages in 55ms
 + numpy==2.5.5
 + palmerpenguins==0.1.6
 + pandas==3.1.1
 + python-dateutil==4.0.0
 + tzdata==2026.6
```

Their environment now matches yours exactly,
down to the version number of a package neither of you has heard of.

If you have ever cloned a project and run `uv sync`,
you have been on the receiving end of this.
Somebody else built an environment,
`uv.lock` wrote down exactly what it contained,
and that one command reproduced it on your computer.
In your own projects you are the person on the other end,
building the environment that someone else will sync.

`uv sync` is the command you will run most often when working with others.
Run it any time you clone a repository with a lockfile in it,
and after every `git pull` that touched `uv.lock`.

### One download, many environments

When we ran `uv sync` it showed
five packages installed in 55 milliseconds,
and nothing was downloaded.
That computer had already downloaded those versions for another project.
Your collaborator's first `uv sync` downloads them once,
and their later projects reuse that download the same way.

Over time you will have a `.venv` in every project
and every bit of scratch work you keep,
and a good number of them will contain the same `pandas`.
Those are not separate copies of it.

`uv` keeps one cache of every version of every package
it has ever downloaded for you:

```bash
uv cache dir
```

```out
/Users/you/.cache/uv
```

A package is downloaded into that cache once.
When a project needs one that is already in there,
`uv` does not copy it into that project's `.venv`.
It uses the cheapest thing the filesystem offers:

- a **copy-on-write clone** on macOS and Linux
- a **hard link** on Windows

That choice is uv's
[`link-mode`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/reference/settings/#link-mode)
setting, and you will almost certainly never need to change it.

Either way the file appears inside the `.venv`
while sharing its blocks on disk with the cached original,
so the second environment costs close to nothing.

The effect is easy to measure.
A freshly synced environment with JupyterLab
in it reports as 164 MB:

```bash
du -sh .venv
```

```out
164M    .venv
```

Sync a *second* project that needs those same versions,
and the free space on the disk drops by a few megabytes, not 164.

Two things follow from this that are worth knowing:

- **The first `uv sync` for a set of packages is the slow one**,
  because it is the one doing the downloading.
  Every later `uv sync` that wants the same versions is close to instant.
- **Deleting a `.venv` is cheap and safe.**
  If an environment gets into a strange state,
  `rm -rf .venv` followed by `uv sync`
  rebuilds it from the cache in seconds.
  That is a reasonable *first* thing to try,
  and it is not something you would casually do
  to a conda environment.

The cache does grow over time.
You can look at it, and tidy it up, with:

```bash
uv cache size --human
uv cache prune
```

`uv cache prune` removes entries nothing points at any more.
`uv cache clean` empties the cache completely,
after which the next `uv sync` downloads everything again.

### Sync makes the environment *match*, in both directions

It is worth being precise about what "sync" means,
because it is stronger than "install".
Suppose someone installs a package directly,
bypassing `uv add`:

```bash
uv pip install cowsay
```

```out
Resolved 1 package in 9ms
Installed 1 package in 3ms
 + cowsay==6.1
```

`cowsay` is now in the environment
but it is not in `pyproject.toml` and not in `uv.lock`.
The environment and the lockfile disagree.
The next `uv sync` resolves that disagreement
in favor of the lockfile:

```bash
uv sync
```

```out
Resolved 6 packages in 4ms
Uninstalled 1 package in 2ms
 - cowsay==6.1
```

`uv sync` installs what is missing **and removes what does not belong**.
This is a feature, not a surprise.
It means an environment you built with `uv sync`
contains exactly what the lockfile says and nothing else,
which is the only way "it works on my machine" can be a meaningful claim.

The lesson is to add packages with `uv add`, not `uv pip install`.
The `uv pip` subcommands exist so that older tutorials and scripts keep working,
but anything installed that way is invisible to your project files.

:::{.activity}
Your collaborator pulls your latest changes and gets
an `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'matplotlib'`
when running your script.
You added `matplotlib` to the project yesterday.
What should they run?

A.  `pip install matplotlib`
B.  `uv sync`
C.  `uv init`
D.  `uv add matplotlib`

:::

## Managing packages

Once a project is shared,
you keep it up to date with a handful of commands.

### Seeing what is installed

`uv tree` shows you the packages you asked
for and what each of them dragged in:

```bash
uv tree
```

```out
Resolved 6 packages in 4ms
penguin-analysis v0.1.0
├── palmerpenguins v0.1.6
│   ├── numpy v2.5.5
│   └── pandas v3.1.1
│       ├── numpy v2.5.5
│       └── python-dateutil v4.0.0
│           └── tzdata v2026.6
└── pandas v3.1.1 (*)
(*) Package tree already displayed
```

The indentation tells the story.
We asked for `palmerpenguins` and `pandas`,
and `numpy`, `python-dateutil`, and `tzdata` are along for the ride.
This is the difference between `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock`,
drawn as a picture.

For a flat list of what is actually in the environment,
`uv pip list` works the way you would expect:

```bash
uv pip list
```

```out
Package         Version
--------------- -------
numpy           2.5.5
palmerpenguins  0.1.6
pandas          3.1.1
python-dateutil 4.0.0
tzdata          2026.6
```

### Removing a package

```bash
uv remove pandas
```

```out
Resolved 6 packages in 9ms
Checked 5 packages in 0.74ms
```

This drops the line from `pyproject.toml`
and updates `uv.lock`.
Notice that nothing was uninstalled.
`palmerpenguins` still needs `pandas`,
so `pandas` stays in the environment as one of its dependencies.
The tree above shows why.

Remove the package that needed it,
and `uv` uninstalls everything that nothing else needs any more:

```bash
uv remove palmerpenguins
```

```out
Resolved 1 package in 5ms
Uninstalled 5 packages in 215ms
 - numpy==2.5.5
 - palmerpenguins==0.1.6
 - pandas==3.1.1
 - python-dateutil==4.0.0
 - tzdata==2026.6
```

One command keeps `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`, and `.venv/` in step.

The rest of this chapter uses both packages, so add them back:

```bash
uv add pandas palmerpenguins
```

```out
Resolved 6 packages in 6ms
Installed 5 packages in 34ms
 + numpy==2.5.5
 + palmerpenguins==0.1.6
 + pandas==3.1.1
 + python-dateutil==4.0.0
 + tzdata==2026.6
```

### Upgrading a package

Your lockfile pins exact versions on purpose,
so `uv sync` will not silently upgrade anything.
When you *do* want a newer version,
ask for it:

```bash
uv lock --upgrade-package pandas
```

This re-resolves just that package,
leaving everything else pinned where it is,
and writes the change into `uv.lock`.
Then `uv sync` to apply it.

Commit the resulting change to `uv.lock`.
A diff on a lockfile is a record of exactly what changed in your environment
and when,
which is a useful thing to have
when a project that worked last month stops working today.

### Dependency groups

Some packages are needed to *develop* the project
but not to *run* it,
such as a test runner, a linter, or a formatter.
These go in a dependency group rather than the main list:

```bash
uv add --dev pytest
```

```{.toml filename="pyproject.toml"}
[project]
name = "penguin-analysis"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = [
    "palmerpenguins>=0.1.6",
    "pandas>=3.1.1",
]

[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "pytest>=9.2.0",
]
```

`uv sync` installs the `dev` group by default,
which is what you want on your own machine.

:::{.callout-note}
Groups are optional,
and for a data analysis project you often do not need them.
This book's own `pyproject.toml` deliberately keeps everything
in a single `dependencies` list
so that there is exactly one install command to remember.

You will meet dependency groups again
in the [packaging chapters](1110-packaging.qmd),
where the distinction between
"what my users need" and "what I need to develop this"
starts to matter a great deal.
:::
